problem: End-to-end deep RL from pixels has high sample complexity and yields brittle policies that fail under mild visual shifts. Domain randomization, the usual fix, complicates learning and can collapse on hard tasks.
motivation: Real deployment (sim-to-real, new textures/objects) never matches training exactly, so policies need built-in invariances. Mid-level vision features from CV objectives (normals, segmentation, depth, etc.) are trained asynchronously on static data; the paper asks whether they scale to hard manipulation and to real-robot navigation, where earlier studies only covered simulated navigation.
key_idea: Feed frozen, asynchronously pretrained mid-level visual encoders (e.g. surface normals, segmentation) as the perceptual state to an RL policy, instead of raw pixels, ground-truth state, or domain randomization.
insight: Mid-level features both simplify learning (higher train success, faster convergence, less hyperparameter sensitivity) and align train/test distributions (better generalization). Table: on Pick+Place, scratch gets 0% train/0% test with or without domain randomization, whereas surface normals get 100%/100%. Domain randomization even lowers scratch train success on Reach (100% to 70%), while mid-level stays near-perfect, so it scales better to harder tasks. Feature usefulness depends on the task but is stable across environments (Spearman rho=0.77 sim vs real).
method: Frozen mid-level encoder: ResNet-50 networks trained offline on Taskonomy-style vision objectives (normals, segmentation, depth, denoising, curvature etc.) transform each image into a latent (16x16x8) fed to the policy; only the policy is updated
Fine-tuning for manipulation: the pretrained encoders are fine-tuned offline on images from the RLBench simulator to close the domain gap, then frozen

Manipulation RL: TD3 + HER on RLBench Reach, Push, Pick+Place with a Franka Panda, sparse rewards, 50-step episodes, continuous XYZ+gripper end-effector deltas; hyperparameters tuned for the scratch baseline (biased against mid-level)
Navigation sim-to-real: PPO point-nav policies from Sax et al. trained in a single Gibson building, deployed zero-shot on a TurtleBot with RGB camera and IMU in unseen real buildings
Baselines: tabula rasa (AtariNet on RGB), blind (zero input), ground-truth state, and domain randomization of textures during training
Analysis: performance vs. mid-level checkpoint quality, and feature rank stability across sim/real (Spearman correlation)

setting.backbone: Frozen ResNet-50 mid-level encoders (Taskonomy-derived, fine-tuned on sim images) + small policy network trained with TD3+HER (manipulation) or PPO (navigation)
setting.training_data: Encoders: Taskonomy-pretrained then fine-tuned on RLBench images; policies: RL in RLBench tabletop (450k steps for Pick+Place) and a single Gibson building for navigation
setting.observation: Monocular RGB (64x64 for scratch; mid-level 16x16x8 latents) plus odometry/IMU for point-goal; no depth/LiDAR for the real robot
setting.action_space: Manipulation: continuous XYZ+gripper end-effector deltas; navigation: discrete {forward, pivot right, pivot left}
setting.simulator: RLBench (CoppeliaSim/PyRep) and Gibson (Habitat) for point navigation
setting.privileged: none (ground-truth state used only for the state baseline)

numbers.eval_set_note: 24 scenarios in two unseen real buildings, 594 evaluation runs
numbers.backbone: Frozen mid-level encoder + PPO policy (Sax et al. 2019), trained in one Gibson building
numbers.extra: zero-shot sim-to-real, no fine-tuning; best feature selected
numbers.evidence: Agents using mid-level features achieved a significantly higher SPL of 0.608 and a completion rate of 0.7.

numbers.extra: held-out textures at test; sparse reward

numbers_note: Not a standard VLN/ObjNav benchmark; manipulation bars for Reach/Push/Pick+Place mostly only in figures. Scratch real-robot: SPL 0.319, completion 0.4.
results: Mid-level agents reach 100% train/test on Pick+Place where scratch and domain-randomized scratch get 0%, and 100% vs 20% on Reach with unseen colors against domain randomization. In real-world zero-shot navigation they achieve SPL 0.608 vs 0.319 for scratch (+90.6%), and converge within about 2x the steps of the state oracle.
limitations: Encoders are frozen and need fine-tuning on simulator images for manipulation; mid-level networks are still susceptible to domain shift
Which feature works best depends on the task and is picked manually; no generic feature selection is explored
Sim-to-real is tested only for navigation, not manipulation; tasks are relatively simple with fixed objects
builds_on: Mid-level vision for visuomotor policies (Sax et al. 2019)
